claims.text: Operational temperatures typical of fusion plasma-facing components are at or above 1200 °C.
High-temperature plastic strain in tungsten-based structural materials is governed mainly by vacancy-diffusion-controlled dislocation climb.
High-temperature toughness in tungsten-based structural materials is governed partly by concurrent grain-boundary sliding.
Enhanced vacancy mobility enables dislocations to bypass obstacles by climb.
Vacancy-enabled dislocation climb lowers the effective yield strength and permits greater plastic deformation.
Grain-boundary sliding redistributes local stresses and alleviates stress concentrations at grain junctions.
Stress redistribution by grain-boundary sliding improves toughness.
Dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding are both sensitive to vacancy concentration and mobility.
Rhenium can serve as a vacancy-stabilizing dopant in tungsten-based material.
Changing the annealing treatment can adjust the vacancy concentration.
Doping or optimized annealing can enhance vacancy mobility while other relevant microstructural variables are held constant.
Samples with enhanced vacancy mobility will have lower yield strength than an undoped, standard-annealed baseline.
Samples with enhanced vacancy mobility will sustain greater plastic strain before failure than the baseline.
Samples with enhanced vacancy mobility will absorb more energy before fracture than the baseline.
Samples with enhanced vacancy mobility will show more microscopic evidence of dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding than the baseline.
The proposed mechanism should hold in refractory metals such as tungsten when vacancy-mediated climb and grain-boundary sliding dominate deformation.
At lower temperatures, dislocation glide dominates rather than vacancy-mediated climb and grain-boundary sliding.
At extremely fine nanoscale grain sizes, grain-boundary diffusion or superplastic flow may become important and limit applicability of the proposed mechanism.
Transient thermal gradients and irradiation-induced defects could complicate the relationship between vacancy mobility and mechanical performance.
Failure to observe both systematic mechanical-property changes and correlated increases in climb or grain-boundary sliding after changing vacancy mobility would falsify the hypothesis.
